meta.subtitle: Cost control lifted margins and the 2026 EPS range; flat sales, a soft production outlook and a deep cyclical downside keep us at HOLD

advisories: model vs Street expected return diverge by 125pp — informational, not scored

analystSentiment.commentary:
BorgWarner's second quarter of 2026 was a margin story on flat sales. Net sales barely moved year over year, yet the U.S. GAAP operating margin reached 10.1%, which the August 5, 2026 release credits to the company's "continued focus on cost controls" in "a lower industry production environment." The same day the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS range on the back of first-half share repurchases and held its sales, margin and cash flow expectations.

At $63.36 the shares pay 12.1x consensus EPS for the current year. That is a fair price for earnings that are still growing, but the company's own outlook has global industry production flat to down 3% in 2026, and the stock has traded far lower within the past year. We hold the current-year multiple in our Base, set the Bear at the 52-week low and land at HOLD; the label turns on how deep the Bear is, not on how we weight it.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
BorgWarner Inc. makes propulsion technology for combustion, hybrid and electric vehicles. The 10-Q MD&A says it sells "primarily to original equipment manufacturers ("OEMs") of light vehicles," and also to commercial-vehicle and off-highway OEMs, to tier one suppliers and into the aftermarket, and describes it as "an original equipment supplier to nearly every major automotive OEM in the world." The company tearsheet lists products from turbochargers, chain systems and transmission components to inverters, eMotors and battery packs. The company was founded in 1928, is headquartered in Auburn Hills, Michigan, and reports on a calendar year.

The MD&A reports four segments: Turbos & Thermal Technologies, Drivetrain & Morse Systems, PowerDrive Systems and Battery Energy Systems. The last was renamed from Battery & Charging Systems in Q1 2026, after the company decided in February 2025 to exit its charging business. eProducts, which the company counts as all products used on or for electric vehicles plus the same products in hybrid powertrains whose technologies carry over, were approximately $663 million, or 18% of total revenue, in the second quarter of 2026.

For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, net sales were $3,648 million, up approximately 0.3% year over year, and U.S. GAAP diluted EPS rose to $1.34 from $1.03.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: BorgWarner is turning flat sales into higher margins and a smaller share count, and the August 5, 2026 guidance raise rests on those two levers rather than on volume. The next year tests whether that can continue while the company expects global industry production to be flat to down 3% in 2026 and Battery Energy Systems sales to keep falling. At $63.36, consensus earnings growth into FY27 at an unchanged current-year multiple gives a moderate gain, while a cyclical turn that cuts both earnings and the multiple would cost much more than that gain. Free cash flow and modest net debt limit the damage but do not remove it. That asymmetry, not the quality of the quarter, sets our HOLD (see Valuation).

catalysts: Third-quarter results: an early test of whether the second half supports the raised 2026 adjusted EPS range of $5.05 to $5.30 (see Growth).
Tariff refunds: the company has begun receiving refunds of tariffs the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated but has booked no receivable, so recoveries would be upside to reported results (see Growth).
Repurchases: the board enlarged the authorization to approximately $1.35 billion, intended to run through 2029 (see Management).
Power generation: the company expects industrial solutions sales of approximately $300 million in 2027, a line the MD&A names among its long-term growth drivers (see Growth).
risks: Industry production: the company's own 2026 outlook already allows for a decline, and a deeper fall in 2027 is the core of our Bear (see Valuation).
Battery Energy Systems: sales are guided down by approximately $250 million in 2026, and the 10-K warns of further losses on EV investments if adoption stays slow (see Risks).
Cost recovery: the company expects more volatile commodity and input costs in 2026 and must recover them from OEM customers through negotiation (see Risks).
Downside range: the shares traded as low as $40.50 within the past 52 weeks, the level our Bear uses (see Valuation).

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Second-quarter 2026 net sales were $3,648 million, up approximately 0.3% year over year on a U.S. GAAP basis and down approximately 1.2% organically. The MD&A breaks the change into three parts: currencies added approximately $54 million, customer recoveries relating to tariffs added approximately $11 million, and unfavorable volume, mix and net new business subtracted approximately $55 million, "primarily due to" an approximately 1% decrease in weighted average market production and lower Battery Energy Systems sales. The release adds that, excluding the Battery Energy Systems decline, organic net sales "were up modestly."

Margins carried the quarter. Gross margin rose to 19.8% from 17.6%; the MD&A attributes the gain primarily to purchasing savings together with lower volume, mix and net new business (approximately $85 million less cost of sales), restructuring savings and reduced depreciation, partly offset by approximately $44 million of currency-driven cost. U.S. GAAP operating margin rose {+220 basis points+} to 10.1% and adjusted operating margin rose {+100 basis points+} to 11.3%. U.S. GAAP diluted EPS rose to $1.34 from $1.03, and adjusted EPS rose {+17.4%+} to $1.42 from $1.21, which the release attributes primarily to higher adjusted operating income and a lower share count from 2025 and 2026 repurchases. The effective tax rate was 22%, up from 18%; the 2025 quarter included discrete tax benefits.

The annual history is weaker than the quarter. GAAP operating margin, around 8% from FY21 to FY23, fell to 3.9% in FY24 and 3.7% in FY25, and FY25 diluted EPS was $1.28. That FY25 figure is below the $1.75 the release reports for the six months ended June 30, 2025 alone, so the second half of 2025 was a GAAP loss; the excerpts we draw on do not itemize it. That loss falls inside the trailing twelve months and helps explain why the trailing operating margin, 5.0%, sits well below the second quarter's. We judge earnings power on the 2026 quarters and the guidance rather than on the trailing figures.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
At December 31, 2025, BorgWarner held $2.3B of cash and short-term investments and $3.9B of total debt, for net debt of $1.6B, down from $2.8B at the end of FY22. The current ratio was 2.07 at that year-end, and the trailing figure is 2.13. Trailing interest coverage is 7.4x, and net interest expense was $10 million in the second quarter of 2026, down from $12 million. The documents we draw on carry no June 30, 2026 balance sheet and the trailing net debt to EBITDA line is blank, so we judge leverage on the year-end figures.

Total equity fell from $7.5B in FY22 to $5.6B in FY25. Most of the decline came in FY23, when equity was $6.1B, the year of the tax-free spin-off of the former Fuel Systems and Aftermarket segments that the release mentions; the excerpts do not quantify its effect, so we note the timing only. One smaller item sits in receivables: approximately $23 million from the October 15, 2025 settlement with PHINIA is due no later than December 1, 2026.

The balance sheet does not constrain the dividend or the buyback at year-end 2025 levels, and it is not the source of our caution; in a downturn, cash generation matters more for this company than leverage does.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Free cash flow was $1.2B in FY25 after capital expenditure of $469 million. The second quarter of 2026 produced operating cash flow of $586 million and free cash flow of $492 million. The August 5 guidance calls for 2026 operating cash flow of $1,600 million to $1,700 million and free cash flow of $900 million to $1,100 million. The release excerpt does not define the company's free cash flow measure, so we treat the comparison with the vendor's FY25 figure as indicative only; on that reading the company expects less free cash flow in 2026 than in FY25.

The trailing FCF yield of 9.4% is the main support for the shares in a downturn, and it funds the repurchases discussed under Management. It is also a trailing figure: the company's own 2026 range points lower, and FY23, a year of heavier capital expenditure, shows the free cash flow margin at 4.0%. We count on cash generation to cushion a downturn, not to prevent one.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The three P/E figures on the page measure different things. The trailing P/E of 31.2x is consistent with U.S. GAAP diluted EPS over the four quarters to June 30, 2026, a window that still holds the second-half 2025 loss (see Financials), so it overstates what buyers pay for current earnings. The forward P/E the vendor labels NTM, 12.1x, lines up with consensus FY26 EPS of $5.22, so we read it as a current-year multiple; the 10.7x forward P/E is on consensus FY27 EPS of $5.93. Both consensus figures are on the company's adjusted basis: the FY26 figure sits inside the adjusted 2026 range (see Growth) and above the U.S. GAAP range of $4.72 to $4.94. The release says the company "defines adjusted earnings per diluted share as earnings per diluted share adjusted to eliminate the impact of restructuring expense, merger, acquisition and divestiture expense, other net expenses, discontinued operations and other gains and losses not reflective of the Company's ongoing operations and related tax effects." Restructuring expense appears in both the 2026 and the 2025 second quarters, so part of what the adjusted figure removes recurs, and we read the forward multiples with that caveat.

On other measures the shares trade at 6.9x trailing EV/EBITDA and 0.9x sales. The Street is more constructive than we are: 11 of 15 analysts rate the shares Buy, and the consensus target of $81.53 sits 28.7% above the price, within a range of $62.00 to $95.00. The price itself has swung widely: the 52-week range runs from $40.50 to $78.82, and $63.36 sits well below the high. No document we draw on explains either end of that range, and we assign no cause.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: FY27 adjusted EPS comes in ahead of consensus as tariff refunds, power generation industrial solutions sales and continued repurchases add to it, and the market pays the Street's consensus target of $81.53. Anchor: the consensus target. Condition: an earnings beat plus a multiple above the current-year level the Base holds.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Consensus FY27 EPS of $5.93 arrives and, with 2027 as the current year, the shares keep the 12.1x they pay today on current-year consensus EPS. Anchor: consensus FY27 EPS at today's current-year multiple. Condition: production steadies, Battery Energy Systems stops shrinking the total, and the 2026 cost actions carry into 2027.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Industry production falls further in 2027, Battery Energy Systems keeps shrinking and commodity or tariff costs go unrecovered, so adjusted EPS falls below the $5.05 floor of the 2026 range, and the multiple drops below the 10.7x the shares pay on FY27 consensus today. Anchor: the 52-week low of $40.50, a price the market paid within the past year. Condition: lower earnings and a lower multiple together.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
We weight Bull 20%, Base 60% and Bear 20%, for a probability-weighted value of $67.46, expected upside of +6.5%, bear-case downside of 36.1% and reward/risk of 0.18×. The rule derives HOLD.

The Base carries most of the weight because the evidence on 2027 leans toward growth without proving it. In its favor, adjusted EPS rose to $2.66 from $2.32 in the six months to June 30, 2026, the August 5 guidance moved up, the charging exit and the North American battery consolidation were each expected to deliver their savings by the end of 2026, and new awards begin production in 2026 and 2027 (see Growth). Against it, the documents give no 2027 company outlook, and the consensus revenue recovery follows a year the company expects to be down organically.

The Bull's weight matches the Bear's because its path needs both a beat and a higher multiple, and its sources of upside, tariff refunds and power generation sales, are unrecognized or a year away. The Bear's weight rests on the Bear's own evidence: the company's 2026 production outlook reaches down 3% at its low end, Battery Energy Systems is guided lower, and the company expects more volatile input costs. Against that, the second quarter showed margins rising while production fell, which keeps a downturn out of the central case.

The label is not sensitive to the weights. BUY needs reward/risk of 0.50× as well as 10% expected upside, and with the Bear that far below the price no split that keeps a fifth of the weight on the Bear gets there; SELL would need the Bear's weight more than doubled. The label is sensitive to the Bear's depth: a Bear only as deep as the desk's minimum would derive BUY at these weights. We put the Bear at the 52-week low because our downturn cuts earnings and the multiple together and the market has paid that price within the past year. That is our judgment and the call's main exposure; a reader who expects a milder downturn would reach BUY on the same evidence.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor data shows one consolidated line and describes BorgWarner as a single reportable segment; the 10-Q MD&A reports four reportable segments, and we follow the MD&A. We do not quote a geographic split. In the second quarter of 2026, Turbos & Thermal Technologies had net sales of $1,442 million (39.5% of net sales) and Drivetrain & Morse Systems $1,455 million (39.9%). Year over year, PowerDrive Systems grew to $665 million from $581 million and Battery Energy Systems fell to $100 million from $159 million, while Turbos & Thermal Technologies slipped and Drivetrain & Morse Systems edged up. Segment figures are before inter-segment eliminations. Growth in PowerDrive Systems offset the Battery Energy Systems decline, but the two segments that make up most of sales were roughly flat, so the total cannot grow much until production does.

moatFactors.name: Program incumbency
moatFactors.body: Awards are won years ahead of revenue: the August 5, 2026 release lists awards with production starting from the fourth quarter of 2026 through 2029, including a "program life extension award" with a European premium OEM and two inverter "extension awards." Extensions show an incumbent position being renewed. The release gives no award values, backlog or win rate, so we cannot size how much revenue this protects.

moatFactors.name: Customer reach
moatFactors.body: The breadth described in the company overview spreads program risk across many OEMs and across light vehicles, commercial vehicles, off-highway and the aftermarket. Reach is not leverage: the release lists "our reliance on major OEM customers" and "competitive challenges from existing and new competitors, including original equipment manufacturer ("OEM") customers" among its risks.

moatFactors.name: Pricing power
moatFactors.body: Gross margin stayed between 18.1% and 18.8% from FY21 to FY25, a narrow band that shows neither erosion nor pricing gains. The second quarter's improvement came from the cost factors discussed under Financials, and the company relies on negotiation to pass through commodity and tariff costs (see Risks). We see no evidence of price leadership in the documents.

moatFactors.name: Powertrain breadth
moatFactors.body: The portfolio spans combustion, hybrid and electric vehicles, which the MD&A calls "particularly critical as the automotive industry continues to see electric vehicle adoption volatility across different regions." Breadth lets the company sell into whichever powertrain gains in a region. It also spreads investment across three technology paths, and returns on the electric path are the risk the 10-K flags (see Risks).

businessMoat.durability: We rate the moat NONE. Program incumbency and reach are real, but the figures we have do not show them earning the returns a moat implies: FY25 net income of $277M sat against total equity of $5.6B, and GAAP operating margin has not exceeded 8.2% in any of the five fiscal years shown. The 2026 guidance for a U.S. GAAP operating margin of 9.6% to 9.8% would sit above that history; if margins at that level hold through a production downturn, that would be evidence for a NARROW rating. The threat to durability is the powertrain transition, and the 10-K lists "technology changes that could render our products obsolete" among the ways the strategy could fail.

points: Sales guidance (August 5, 2026): net sales "in the range of $14.0 billion to $14.3 billion in 2026, compared with 2025 net sales of approximately $14.3 billion," with organic net sales down 3.5% to down 1.5%. The range assumes weighted light vehicle markets down 3% to approximately flat, an approximately $250 million decline in Battery Energy Systems sales (approximately a 1.7% headwind to organic growth) and approximately $175 million of currency tailwind. At best, 2026 sales are flat, and only because of currency.

EPS guidance: the same release raised adjusted EPS to $5.05 to $5.30 from $5.00 to $5.20, "due to the impact of the Company's share repurchases during the first half of 2026," and kept the adjusted operating margin range at 10.7% to 10.9%. The raise is real but financial, not operational. Consensus FY26 EPS of $5.22 sits in the upper half of the new range, so the Street already assumes delivery toward the top.

New business: the release lists an eTurbo award for a hybrid passenger car (production from 2029), a transfer case for a Chinese OEM's newly developed full-size SUV (fourth quarter of 2026), two variable cam timing awards (2026 and 2027), an Integrated Drive Modules award with a global OEM (2027) and two high-volume inverter extension awards for plug-in hybrid and battery-electric vehicles (2029). The awards span combustion, hybrid and electric programs, but the release gives no values, so they support the long-term case without moving our 2027 numbers.

Power generation: the MD&A expects power generation industrial solutions sales of approximately $300 million in 2027, and the release says the company plans to increase 2026 R&D spending to accelerate data center and industrial opportunities. It is a sized new line, but small next to group sales, and the extra R&D is a 2026 cost ahead of 2027 revenue.

Tariff refunds: the company has begun to receive refunds of tariffs levied under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which the U.S. Supreme Court invalidated on February 20, 2026. It recognized no refund receivable at June 30, 2026 because "the ultimate recoverability, timing and amount of any such refund amounts remain uncertain." Refunds are upside the company has not quantified, and we count them only in the Bull.

2027 recovery: consensus expects FY27 revenue of $14.8B, up from $14.2B for FY26E. The company has not guided 2027 sales beyond power generation, and eProduct revenue was approximately $1,260 million in the six months to June 30, 2026, down from $1,295 million, so the recovery consensus assumes is not yet visible in the electrified business. We treat it as plausible but unproven, and it is the Base's main exposure.

management.leadership: The proxy excerpt (DEF 14A, filed March 19, 2026) names the executive officers in the Summary Compensation Table, Joseph F. Fadool, Craig D. Aaron, Stefan Demmerle, Volker Weng and Tonit M. Calaway, but gives no titles or tenures, so we assign no roles. It notes that Mr. Lissalde retired from the Company on February 6, 2025. Separately, the August 5, 2026 release lists CEO transition compensation among the non-comparable items in its EPS reconciliation, which indicates a change of chief executive; the excerpts do not say who left or who succeeded. We therefore judge management on the evidence in the filings: a margin gain in a quarter of lower production, the February 2025 decisions to exit charging and consolidate the North American battery systems business, and a raised EPS range. Execution on cost has been good. The harder test is investment timing, which the 10-K (February 11, 2026) puts plainly: "Our future success is dependent upon us making the right investments at the right times, with the right customers who can rapidly adapt to the market."
management.capitalAllocation: Repurchases dominate shareholder returns. In FY25 the company bought back $508 million of stock and paid $119 million of dividends; in the second quarter of 2026 it repurchased approximately $100 million and paid a $34 million dividend. On August 5, 2026 the board raised the authorization by $1 billion to approximately $1.35 billion, "intended to allow management to repurchase the Company's outstanding shares through 2029." Diluted weighted average shares fell to 206.3 million in the quarter from 218.2 million a year earlier, and the release credits the lower count for part of the adjusted EPS gain. The MD&A also calls acquisitions "an integral component of the Company's growth and value creation strategy." Buying stock at 10.7x FY27 consensus earnings is sound if that consensus holds; the cost is a thinner cushion if production falls, and acquisitions carry the impairment exposure discussed under Risks.
management.governance: The same proxy excerpt covers share ownership only. It does not show board composition, director independence, committees or pay design, so we make no claim about them. As of December 31, 2025, the holders reported above five percent were The Vanguard Group at 12.1%, BlackRock, Inc. at 9.0%, BlackRock Portfolio Management at 7.3% and Dimensional Fund Advisors LP at 5.5%; Dimensional's figure rests on a Schedule 13G reporting holdings as of December 31, 2024, so it is the oldest line in the table. None of these holders is near control. Vanguard reported shared voting power over 1,678,368 of its 24,974,138 shares, so its votable stake is far smaller than its economic one. With no controlling holder, accountability runs through the board, and the excerpt gives us no basis to judge that board either way.
management.insiderOwnership: As of March 3, 2026, the directors and executive officers as a group (17 persons) beneficially owned 1,556,923 shares, less than one percent of the 206,061,488 shares outstanding, including 722,194 shares of unvested restricted stock. Joseph F. Fadool's 434,964 shares, including 163,796 unvested restricted shares, exceed every other individual holding listed. Each listed director's total includes 5,814 shares of unvested restricted stock. Insider stakes are small against the share count, so alignment rests on restricted stock rather than on large personal holdings. The excerpt does not say whether those awards vest on time or on performance, and we do not characterize them.

idiosyncratic: Electrification investments. The 10-K (February 11, 2026) warns that if EV adoption "continues to be slower as compared to our expectations, we may not only fail to realize expected rates of return on our existing investments, we may also incur further losses on such investments." Battery Energy Systems is already shrinking and eProduct revenue was lower in the six months to June 30, 2026 than a year earlier (see Growth), so this risk is live rather than hypothetical.

Impairments and acquisitions. The 10-K says goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets "represent a significant portion of our total assets" and refers to impairment charges recorded for 2025 and 2024. It adds that the risk "is higher during the early years following an acquisition." With acquisitions part of the strategy (see Management), each new deal restarts that exposure; an impairment would hit GAAP earnings and equity, though not cash.

Cost recovery from OEMs. The MD&A expects commodity prices and other input costs to show "a higher level of volatility in 2026 compared to 2025," and the release lists "an inability to achieve expected levels of recoverability in commercial negotiations with customers" among its risks. Tariff recoveries from customers helped second-quarter sales (see Financials), but they are negotiated, not automatic, and a shortfall would come straight out of the margin gains the thesis relies on.
risks.systemic: Auto production is the main macro exposure. The MD&A states that "automotive and truck production is cyclical and sensitive to general economic conditions and other factors, including interest rates, consumer credit and consumer spending and preferences," and that declines which materially reduce production "would have an adverse effect on the Company's sales." The company already assumes a weaker 2026 (see Growth). Currency is the second exposure: a stronger Euro and Chinese Renminbi lifted both second-quarter sales and the 2026 guide, and a reversal would take that support away. Policy is the third: the MD&A notes that changes in tariffs, including retaliatory tariffs, and the start or end of consumer incentives such as EV tax credits "may affect consumer preferences." Execution cannot offset these, which is why our Bear is a cyclical turn rather than a company-specific failure.

body: HOLD, target range $60–$75, against a price of $63.36. BorgWarner executed well in the second quarter and raised its EPS range, but the raise came from repurchases, sales are guided flat to lower, and the year ahead depends on an industry the company expects to be flat to lower in 2026. Our weighted value of $67.46 sits a little above the price. The Base gain is moderate, and the Bear is deep enough that reward/risk stays well short of what a BUY needs; as Valuation sets out, the label depends on the Bear's depth rather than on its weight.

We would upgrade to BUY if the company's first 2027 outlook, or its second-half 2026 results, show adjusted EPS growth with production holding up, because that evidence would let us set a shallower Bear, and a Bear near the desk's minimum depth derives BUY at today's price. We would downgrade to SELL if the shares rose to our Base value of $71.75 before the evidence changed, since at that price our scenarios derive SELL. A guidance cut below the $5.05 floor of the adjusted 2026 range would lower our Base anchor; whether it moves the label depends on how far FY27 consensus follows it down.
